extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalists interested in historical press practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or producing newspapers in the U.S. Civil War and Reconstruction era, emphasizing newsworthiness, editorial style, production constraints, and organizational practices. Focuses on what made papers successful or deficient (e.g., freshness of news, human-interest material, writing quality, censorship and material shortages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness (novelty/unexpectedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is defined by novelty — the text encapsulates the axiom: 'When a dog bites a man, that is not news; but when a man bites a dog, that is news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories that are unexpected, unusual, or counterintuitive. The 'man bites dog' maxim is the operational test of news value; ordinary occurrences are not newsworthy. (Example from the Sun's city desk: look for the surprising angle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness and mass-appeal of news
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun advertised: 'Its news is the freshest, most interesting and sprightliest current, and no expense is spared to make it just what the great mass of the people want.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the freshest, most engaging presentation of current events and tailor selection and tone to what appeals to a broad readership. Investment in gathering and packaging 'fresh' material is recommended; failure to appeal to mass tastes risks circulation loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest feature criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'human-interest story' is 'a little article which was interesting not from the significance of the person or event reported, but because (as in fiction) it was amusing or pathetic or meaningful as a bit of the texture of our universal human life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-interest pieces to illuminate everyday life; their value depends on good, readable writing rather than intrinsic importance of the subject. Avoid banality by ensuring craft and evocative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing quality and stylistic vivacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun's chief contribution was 'good writing—colorful, witty, zestful writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize lively, readable prose across beats: bright copy, wit, and distinct voice increase reader engagement. Editors should recruit and train writers who can produce 'colorful' copy; mere topic selection without craft leads to blandness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style: concision, wit, incisiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials under Dana 'were often short and amusing essays' and displayed 'incisiveness and wit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, pointed editorials that combine clear judgment with lively expression. Short, pithy essays on social and political questions can increase influence. Beware that frivolity or irrelevance can reduce substantive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of malicious/cruel attacks (ethical influence consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dana's Sun could be 'cruel and malicious' in its onslaughts; such blackguardism 'undoubtedly reduced its actual influence to a rather low level.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive personal attacks or gratuitous cruelty may gain attention but harm long-term credibility and influence. Balance sharp criticism with fairness and avoid ad hominem excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational content to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers flourished by being 'pert, novel, and sometimes sensational' and featured 'murders, scandals, society gossip, and the new interview style of story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational items, scandals, and gossip can drive circulation and provide accessible hooks for readers, but must be balanced against credibility and ethics. Explicit examples: murder coverage, society gossip, scandal pieces, interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of interviews as a news form
rubrics_metrics.description: The period saw the rise of 'the new interview style of story' as a distinct feature in popular papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to add immediacy, personality, and direct-source voice. Train reporters in interview technique and integrate interviews into feature and news coverage judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in staff development and newsroom training
rubrics_metrics.description: Dana 'encouraged by good salaries, fairly assured tenure, and an excellent system of training' to recruit 'bright young men' and produce better journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in hiring, training, and retaining competent reporters and editors; provide fair compensation and structured mentorship to improve writing and reporting standards. Organizational commitment to talent development underpinned the Sun's quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical production quality and material constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Southern papers suffered from lack of paper, ink, and printing materials, forcing 'small sizes' and even use of 'wrapping paper or wallpaper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production materials (paper, ink, presses) and format (page count, size) materially affect presentation and perceived quality. Plan formats and pricing with realistic resource assessments; shortages will force reduced format and can harm readability and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business model/price affects format and content depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun's two-cent price competed with four-cent papers that had twice as many pages; pricing and format affected page counts and the amount of editorial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how cover price and revenue model constrain page count and content depth. Low-price competitors can gain circulation but may need to optimize content mix (short pieces, human-interest, sensational items) to succeed within limited space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access, censorship and correspondent freedom determine news quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Confederate and military censorship (e.g., banishing correspondents; criminalizing publication of troop movements) and failures in telegraph/mails produced relatively poor southern news quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom of movement and access to primary sources are central to accuracy and timeliness. Restrictions on correspondents or legal/regulatory censorship degrade the completeness and reliability of reporting. News organizations should seek secure lines of communication and legal awareness to preserve reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational/political alignment and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers often followed party lines (e.g., many northern dailies opposed Johnson; Democratic papers advocated moderate course); ownership and political alignment shaped editorial positions and could cost subscriptions (example: Raymond's involvement in politics cost the Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that explicit political positions and managerial/political entanglements shape credibility and commercial outcomes. Maintaining editorial independence from partisan or personal political risk may preserve broader readership; entanglement can cause subscription and advertising loss.
